In National Federation of Independent Business v. Department of Labor, 
595 U.S. 109 (2022), the Court held that plaintiffs were likely to succeed on 
their claim that the Secretary of Labor violated the Occupational Safety and 
Health Act when he issued an “emergency temporary standard” mandating 
that employers with more than 100 employees require the employees to 
undergo COVID-19 vaccination or take weekly COVID-19 tests. The statute 
authorizes the Secretary to promulgate occupational safety and health 
standards that are “reasonably necessary or appropriate to provide safe or 
healthful employment.” 29 U.S.C. § 655(b). Although the statute ordinarily 
requires notice-and-comment procedures, the Secretary may forgo those 
procedxxres for “emergency temporary standards” upon the showing “that 
employees are exposed to grave danger from exposure to substances or agents 
determined to be toxic or physically harmful or from new hazards” and that 
the standard “is necessary to protect employees from such danger.” § 655(c)(1). 
The Secretary had used the power nine times before the COVID-19 
requirement. In sustaining the challenge, the Court remarked that “[i]t is 
telling that OSHA, in its half century of existence, has never before adopted a 
broad pubhc health regulation of this kind—addressing a threat that is 
untethered in any causal sense, from the workplace.” According to the Court, 
“[t]his ‘lack of historical precedent,’ coupled with the breadth of authority that 
the Secretary now claims, is a ‘telling indication’ that the mandate extends 
beyond the agency’s legitimate reach.” In a concurrence. Justice Gorsuch 
expressly tied this reasoning to the nondelegation doctrine. Justices Breyer, 
Sotomayor, and Kagan jointly dissented.
On the same day that the Court decided the “vaccine or test” case, a 
majority of five justices, without mentioning the major questions doctrine, 
refused to stay a rule issued by the Department of Health and Human Services 
that adopted a vaccination mandate for staff of healthcare facilities 
participating in Medicare and Medicaid. See Biden v. Missouri, 595 U.S. 87 
(2022).
In Alabama Association of Realtors v. Department of Health and Human 
Services, 594 U.S. 758 (2021), the Court addressed a challenge to a nationwide 
eviction moratorium for residential rental properties imposed by the Director 
of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. The Director invoked a 
statute, section 361(a) of the Public Health Service Act, authorizing the 
enforcement of regulations “necessary to prevent the introduction, 
transmission, or spread of communicable disease from foreign countries into 
the States or possessions, or from one State or possession into any other State 
or possession.” 42 U.S.C. § 264(a). In a per curiam opinion, the Court reasoned 
that “[e]ven if the text were ambiguous, the sheer scope of the CDC’s claimed 
authority under § 361(a) would counsel against the Government’s 
interpretation. We expect Congress to speak clearly when authorizing an 
agency to exercise powers of “vast ‘economic and political significancA? ” Again, 
Justices Breyer, Sotomayor, and Kagan dissented.
